units.name: wsgi-app
units.description: This is the heart of Flask: the object you create with `Flask(__name__)` in every Flask program. It remembers all the URL routes, error handlers, and settings you registered, and it is the thing an actual web server (or Flask's own built-in development server) calls for every incoming request. It figures out which piece of your code should handle a request, runs 'before' and 'after' hooks, catches errors and turns them into a proper HTTP response, and can also start a local test server for development. It must never itself decide what a URL 'means' in business terms (that is the job of your view functions) — its job is purely the plumbing that turns an incoming web request into a call to your code and your code's return value into an HTTP response.
units.role: Defines the Flask application object and the request/response dispatch and error-handling machinery that turns WSGI calls into view-function calls.

units.name: scaffold
units.description: This file defines the shared rulebook that both a full Flask application and a Blueprint (a reusable, mountable chunk of an app) use to let developers register things onto them: URL routes, before/after-request hooks, error handlers, template context processors, and so on. It also knows how to figure out where an app's static files and templates live on disk, and how to locate a Python package's folder on the filesystem. It must never let App and Blueprint drift into registering things differently from each other.
units.role: Shared base class providing the route/hook/error-handler registration API and static/template folder resolution used by both App and Blueprint.

units.name: blueprints
units.description: This unit implements Flask's Blueprint feature, which lets a developer split a web application into reusable, self-contained pieces. A Blueprint groups related routes, view functions, static files, and templates together without needing a live application object; it is only wired in when the main app calls register_blueprint. It must never apply its routes to the app before registration, and must correctly apply any URL prefix/subdomain given at registration time.
units.role: Defines the Blueprint and BlueprintSetupState classes that let routes/handlers be declared separately from the app and merged in later.

Blueprint.send_static_file (blueprints.py:82-102) serves files from the blueprint's static folder by delegating to helpers.send_from_directory.

units.name: views
units.description: This code lets a programmer write a web page's logic as a Python class instead of a single function, which is handy when a page needs to handle several kinds of requests (like showing a form on GET and processing it on POST) using clearly named methods. A base View class provides the general mechanism, and a MethodView subclass automatically routes GET/POST/PUT/etc. requests to matching methods. It must never change what a class-based view returns — only decide which method handles the request.
units.role: Provides class-based view dispatch, converting a View/MethodView subclass into the plain callable Flask's routing registers.

entrypoints.name: View.dispatch_request

entrypoints.name: MethodView

units.name: request-context
units.description: This unit is Flask's mechanism for making 'the current app', 'the current request', 'the session', and a per-request scratch space (g) available anywhere in a view function or extension, without passing them around as arguments. When a request (or a CLI command, or a manual app_context() block) begins, an AppContext bundling the app, request, and session is pushed onto a stack-like slot; code elsewhere reads that slot through the current_app/request/session/g/app_ctx proxies. When it ends, the context is popped, teardown callbacks run, and the slot is restored. It must never let one request's state leak into another concurrent or subsequent request.
units.role: Manages the lifecycle (push/pop/teardown) of per-request and per-app ambient state, and exposes read access to it via global proxy objects.

It is the translation layer between a raw WSGI environ and the friendly objects Flask developers use.

units.name: json
units.description: This unit provides Flask's JSON handling: turning Python values (dicts, lists, dataclasses, dates, UUIDs, etc.) into JSON text and back again. It defines a pluggable provider interface so an application can swap in a different JSON library, ships a default implementation built on Python's standard json module, offers simple dumps/loads/jsonify helper functions, and includes a 'tagged JSON' format used to safely pack extra Python types into the signed session cookie.
units.role: Serializes and deserializes JSON data for API responses, files, and session cookies, with a pluggable provider mechanism.

units.name: sessions
units.description: This unit takes the small dictionary of data a request handler stashes in flask.session and turns it into a tamper-proof, timestamped cookie sent to the browser, read back on the next request. It never stores session data on the server; instead it signs the JSON-encoded data with the app's secret key so the browser can hold it but cannot forge or silently modify it. It must never accept session data whose signature fails verification, and must never assume a session is authentic just because a cookie with the right name arrived.
units.role: Signs/verifies the flask.session cookie and defines the pluggable session-storage contract.

units.name: templating

It knows how to find template files in the main application's folder and in the folders belonging to any registered blueprints, so a request for a template name searches all the right places. It provides the functions developers call to turn a template plus data into a finished page, either all at once or streamed piece by piece, and it announces via signals when rendering starts and finishes.

units.name: config
units.description: This is Flask's settings box. Every application keeps its configuration (SECRET_KEY, DEBUG mode, database URLs, session lifetime, custom settings) in a single dict-like Config object. This unit provides that object plus several ways to fill it: from a Python object/class, a Python file on disk, a JSON/TOML file, an environment variable pointing at a file, environment variables with a given prefix, or a plain dictionary. It must never be used to execute untrusted input: from_pyfile executes the target file as Python code, so pointing it at an attacker-controlled path is equivalent to arbitrary code execution.
units.role: Holds and loads an application's runtime configuration from objects, files, and environment variables.

units.name: cli
units.description: This is the command-line tool people run when they type `flask` in a terminal (or `python -m flask`). It figures out which Flask application to load, optionally reads settings from .env/.flaskenv files, and then either starts the built-in development server, opens an interactive Python shell, or prints a table of the app's URL routes. It also provides building blocks (AppGroup, ScriptInfo, with_appcontext, FlaskGroup) other units and end-user projects use to add their own commands.

Alongside it sits a companion file of developer-facing diagnostics: friendly error messages that fire only in debug mode when something is set up wrong. Together these are the utility layer other units reach into, not features in their own right.

units.name: package-exports
units.description: This is the front door of the Flask library: a single file that decides which names become visible to someone who writes `import flask` or `from flask import X`. It contains no logic of its own, just a curated list of re-export statements, but it is the contract between everything Flask's internals do and what an application author is allowed to touch directly. It must never expose internal implementation details that aren't meant for application authors to use.
units.role: Defines Flask's public API surface by re-exporting names from internal modules.

units.name: signals
units.description: This is a simple notice-board that other parts of Flask post to when something noteworthy happens while an application is running, such as a request starting or finishing, an error occurring, a template being rendered, or a flash message being queued. It does nothing on its own except define these named announcement channels; other modules can post to a channel or subscribe to it without calling each other directly.
units.role: Defines Flask's lifecycle event signals (built on the blinker library) that decouple event producers from event subscribers.

violations_observed.note: helpers.py names _split_blueprint_path and _CollectErrors with a leading underscore, the Python convention for 'private, do not import from outside this module', yet wsgi-app, request-context, and http-wrappers all import them directly. They are de facto part of helpers' public contract despite the naming; helpers' entrypoint list includes them so this is at least an honest, not silent, seam, but the underscore prefix invites readers to believe they are safe to change without notice.

Both _cv_app (request-context) and _sentinel (scaffold) are underscore-prefixed module internals that are nonetheless imported directly by other units (debughelpers.py imports _cv_app; blueprints.py imports _sentinel). Same pattern as above: a private-looking name is actually a cross-unit contract.

debughelpers.py (folded into the helpers unit) reaches directly into wsgi-app's App class and blueprints' Blueprint class to do isinstance checks for diagnostic messages. Both App and Blueprint are legitimate listed entrypoints of their units, so this is not a boundary violation in the strict sense, but it does mean helpers' diagnostics will silently stop matching if either class is ever renamed or restructured without updating debughelpers.py in lockstep — a coupling that is easy to miss because the import is deferred (function-local).
